opening.headline: We explore how to trace which models and services are affected by a column change using a lineage approach.
body: Changing or deleting a single column may affect downstream tables, dashboards, and models. However, if you don't know who is using that column, the change can quickly become an incident.

In this lesson, we examine what data lineage is, how to query lineage system tables, and when to use graphs and queries. We then explore a case study of impact analysis before column deletion and verify the limitations of lineage.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the concept and system tables of Lineage.
You can distinguish methods for tracking influence scope using Lineage.

screens.title: I changed the column, but I don't know who's affected.
screens.lead: Before modifying data, let's first consider the most immediate question that comes to mind. Think about what entity you need to verify by reading the scene.

paragraphs: A data engineer has requested that the amount column name in the orders table be changed or deleted. The change itself is a one-line task. The issue is that we do not know who is currently using this column.

Downstream, there may be tables, jobs, dashboards, models, or services that read this column. If changes are made without verification, reports may break or model inputs may be lost, and this issue is only discovered after an incident occurs.

In this situation, what's needed is a map that shows where data originates and where it goes. This map is called a data lineage. In this class, we'll explain the concept of lineage and system tables, and distinguish how to trace impact scopes using lineage.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What downstream targets should be checked before deleting a column? Review the list again when the lesson concludes.

screens.title: How do you perform a data change impact analysis?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: Are you not currently asking the responsible party or searching the code to determine the scope of impact?
items.answer: Many organizations use this approach. However, human memory and retrieval are prone to errors, and usage locations outside of code repositories—such as notebooks or dashboards—are difficult to locate. This course addresses how to fill those gaps by using dependency relationships recorded by the system.

items.prompt: Have you ever encountered a problematic situation where a missed dependency relationship was discovered later?
items.answer: This experience manifests as errors reported downstream after a change has been completed. If dependencies were previously recorded, the issue would have been detectable before the change. The lineage shows what was visible before the change.

items.prompt: Have you ever gone back to the source to investigate when the report numbers appeared abnormal?
items.answer: This is a trace from downstream to upstream. Lines support both directions. The change impact is in the downstream direction, while the root cause trace reads the same map in the upstream direction.

screens.outro: Based on recalled experiences, let's examine what Lineage demonstrates.

screens.title: Data lineage is: a map of sources and flows.
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Data lineage is a map that shows where data comes from and where it goes. Unity Catalog automatically collects lineage for queries executed in Databricks up to Column level and aggregates it across all connected workspaces. The purposes of lineage include Impact Analysis, root cause tracing, sensitive data flow tracking, and understanding team dependencies. Nodes in the graph can represent tables and views, ML models Model Version, External assets, and file paths. Google Cloud's Knowledge Catalog also provides lineage based on the same concept, for purposes such as trust validation, issue resolution, change management, and compliance.

terms.tip: This means tracing not just the entire table, but specifically which column a particular column was derived from. This level of granularity is required for impact analysis when modifying a single column.
An activity performed to identify downstream objects that depend on a table or column before altering it.
A specific version of an ML model can also become a node in a lineage graph, allowing us to track which model uses which data.
This node refers to systems outside of Unity Catalog. External assets registered here will be connected within the graph.
This is a catalog product of Google Cloud. It displays the lineages of products such as BigQuery and Vertex AI through console graphs and APIs.

visual.alt: A lineage graph connecting tables and jobs, dashboards, and model versions with arrows.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the concept, let's now look at how to read this map using a query.

screens.title: Lineage System Table Query
screens.lead: Read the following query from top to bottom, and verify the meaning of each line against the right-hand explanation to check for discrepancies.

data.code:
--Find downstream targets that write values by reading the orders table
SELECT target_table_full_name,
       entity_type,
       created_by,
       event_time
FROM system.access.table_lineage
WHERE source_table_full_name = 'main.sales.orders'
ORDER BY event_time DESC;

--Instead, a query asking about the upstream: swaps source and target.
SELECT source_table_full_name
FROM system.access.table_lineage
WHERE target_table_full_name = 'main.sales.daily_sales';

notes.note: This is a query. It displays the downstream target name, the type of operation that created it, the executing entity, and the timestamp. The query fails if the stream name is incorrect.

The Lineage system tables consist of two. system.access.table_lineage records one row for each read or write event on a UC table or path, while column_lineage records lineage at the column level. These tables are not visible when the system schema is disabled.
This condition keeps only the rows reading this table. If the names of the three parts differ from the actual ones, the result will be zero rows.

This is a sorting that displays recent events first. If entity_type is JOB, NOTEBOOK, PIPELINE, DASHBOARD_V3, etc., it indicates the type of operation that created the downstream task; if NULL, it indicates an event recorded without any associated operation.

If the source and target are swapped, the query becomes an upstream query. Impact analysis proceeds in the downstream direction, while root cause tracing goes in the upstream direction. System tables retain rolling data for one year and only record entries when inference is possible; therefore, a zero-row result does not necessarily mean there is no dependency.

screens.outro: Having read the query, I'll compare the approaches of using a graph versus the query.

screens.title: Graph exploration, query, Knowledge Catalog
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn when each of the three verification methods is appropriate and their limitations.

tabs.label: Graph
tabs.body: The graph in Catalog Explorer is suitable when visually browsing upstream and downstream tables. You can select a node and step through it to verify which operations and dashboards follow. It's fastest when dealing with just a few items, but becomes cumbersome when inspecting multiple tables at once.

tabs.label: System Table
tabs.body: System table queries are appropriate when inspecting multiple tables at once or generating reports. You can retrieve a list of downstream task names and their last execution times and share it with the owning team. Instead, you must write queries, and there is a limitation of one-year retention.

tabs.label: Knowledge Catalog
tabs.body: Knowledge Catalog presents the lineage of services such as BigQuery and Vertex AI in Google Cloud through console graphs and APIs. It is used to achieve the same objectives in environments that do not use Databricks. The underlying concepts are the same, although the verification tools differ. Trust validation, issue resolution, change management, and compliance are all reasons for using lineage. From a change management perspective, the most direct use case is verifying downstream dependencies before a change is made.

tabs.label: Common conditions
tabs.body: To view a lineage, the target catalog must have at least BROWSE permission. Additionally, lineage is collected only from supported query paths, so the absence of a graph does not imply no dependencies. Regardless of the method used, remember these two points: without proper permissions, the graph may appear empty, and even with permissions, usage outside of supported collection paths will not be visible. In either case, interpreting the result as evidence of no dependencies is incorrect.

screens.outro: We have summarized the differences among the three methods; now let's apply this to a column deletion example.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Impact Analysis Before Column Deletion
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of checking the impact scope before deleting the amount column. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: There has been a request to clean up the amount column in the orders table. The goal is to determine whether it is safe to remove the column from all places where it is currently used. The approach involves using a graph along with queries.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify downstream at column level
steps.body: Check downstream of amount at the column level lineage. In this case, two outputs are generated: a daily sales table and a dashboard. By viewing at the column level rather than the table level, you can identify places that only use the amount column.

steps.title: Step 2: List in system table
steps.body: Queries the system table to list the downstream tasks and notebook names along with their last execution times. Items with long last execution times may no longer be in use, and tasks that have been running recently must be reported to the responsible personnel.

steps.title: Step 3: Model Usage Verification
steps.body: Check in the model version node whether the model service is using features created with amount. Since the model may degrade in quality without errors when inputs are lost, issues might not become apparent until after the dashboard.

steps.title: Step 4: Alerts and Concurrent Operations
steps.body: Notify the ownership team and establish the order of operations: first enable the replacement column in parallel, then delete it. The key point is to first open the alternative path and not delete it immediately.

steps.title: Step 5: Vulnerability Remediation
steps.body: Dependency on external tools not captured in Lineage is addressed by registering them as external assets. External assets not registered do not appear in the graph, thus are finalized by confirmation from the responsible team. Results confirmed at this stage should be recorded along with deletion schedules so they can be reused when the same question arises in the future.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: In summary, the deletion in this case is deferred until after parallel operation, rather than being executed immediately. There were two dashboards, a daily revenue table, and a model feature downstream, and external tool dependencies have not yet been verified. A line is not a tool that provides confidence, but rather a tool that creates a list of items to verify.

screens.outro: Since we've confirmed the sequence of impact analysis, let's now examine the areas that a lineage might overlook.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Reading the Vulnerabilities of Lineage
screens.lead: When you select an item, a reason why Lineage might be at risk and how to address it will be displayed. First, try to anticipate it on your own before clicking.

items.prompt: Why might a table read through an alternative path be missing?
items.answer: The lineage is collected when queries are executed via Spark DataFrame or Databricks SQL interface. Lineage for sources read through other paths may not be recorded.

items.prompt: What about unregistered tables and external systems?
items.answer: Tables must be registered in the UC metadata store, and external assets must be registered in external metadata to be connected in the graph. They do not appear on the map prior to registration.

items.prompt: Can quarterly tasks executed long ago be found in the system tables?
items.answer: Since the retention period is rolling one year, older quarterly activities may not be visible. Special attention should be given to activities at the annual level. For example, even if year-end closing activities use this column, records might not exist within the past year. Therefore, impact analysis is concluded by adding confirmation from the responsible team to the lineage results.

items.prompt: If the previous query returned zero rows, what order should we check them in?
items.answer: We check the three items in sequence. First, does the table name exactly match the three-part name consisting of catalog, schema, and table? Second, was the read operation executed within a supported path? Third, is the event within the one-year retention period? If all three checks are satisfied and still returns zero rows, then directly verify with the responsible team.

screens.outro: Now that I understand the weaknesses, I'll summarize today's content.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizing the core of the lecture.

paragraphs: Lines show the map of changes. They display sources and downstream dependencies down to the column level, and querying system tables can produce a list of affected scopes.

Impact analysis should be performed using graphs and queries, while considering the limitations of the data collection scope. Empty results do not prove independence and should be finalized with confirmation from the responsible team.

Going back to the initial question, downstream dependencies to check before deleting a column include tables, jobs, notebooks, dashboards, model versions, and external assets. The basic sequence involves reviewing these items with a graph, creating a list using system tables, and notifying the owning team.

By making this process habitual, you will be able to describe the scope of impact before any change. A good starting point is to include downstream lists and parallel operation plans alongside change requests.

glossary.def: A map that shows data sources, transformations, and consumption paths connected as nodes and links.
Refers to system.access.table_lineage and column_lineage. Read and write events can be queried.
An activity to understand downstream objects that depend on a table or column before making changes.
Google Cloud's catalog product offers lines such as BigQuery and Vertex AI.

misconceptions.myth: If not visible in Lineage, dependency does not exist.
misconceptions.fact: Due to limitations on collection paths, registration conditions, and retention periods, additional confirmation from the responsible team is required.
When checking multiple objects at once, system table queries are advantageous.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: Lines are the guide to change.
Linjiang shows source and downstream dependencies down to the column level.
The impact scope can be queried from the system table to create a list.
Aware of the limitations of the collection scope, further verification with the responsible team is conducted.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the scope of impact when we currently change data?
